presentingComplaint: Palpitations, unintentional weight loss and loose stools noted during pre-operative assessment for an elective hip replacement.
history: A 74-year-old woman on the elective orthopaedic waiting list for a right total hip replacement was referred to the medical team when pre-operative work-up revealed a new irregularly irregular tachycardia. Over the preceding 3 months she has lost about 6 kg despite a preserved appetite, reports frequent palpitations, mild anxiety, heat intolerance and 3-4 loose (non-bloody) stools per day. She denies chest pain, syncope, fever, sore throat, neck pain or recent illness. Her presentation is subacute rather than a decompensated crisis. Background: long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis. Polypharmacy includes amlodipine, ramipril, metformin, atorvastatin and, started 5 months ago by her GP, low-dose amiodarone for symptomatic ectopy. She was commenced on apixaban when the atrial fibrillation was detected at pre-assessment. No prior thyroid disease, no goitre noticed, no eye symptoms. Ex-smoker, minimal alcohol, lives independently.
examination: Alert, orientated and comfortable at rest — not toxic or agitated. Warm peripheries with a fine postural tremor of the outstretched hands. Pulse irregularly irregular ~118/min, wide pulse pressure. No lid lag or proptosis; a small, non-tender, diffuse goitre is palpable without bruit. Chest clear, no signs of heart failure, JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No focal neurology; GCS 15.
imaging: ECG: atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate ~118/min, no acute ischaemic changes. Chest X-ray clear, normal cardiac silhouette. Thyroid ultrasound: diffusely enlarged gland with heterogeneous echotexture; low colour-flow Doppler in keeping with amiodarone effect rather than hypervascular Graves.
microbiology: Not applicable — no infective focus; septic screen not indicated on clinical grounds.
differentialDiagnoses: Thyrotoxicosis (uncomplicated) — most likely; suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3, likely amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis in an elderly polypharmacy patient
Thyroid storm — excluded: Burch-Wartofsky score low, patient afebrile, no CNS dysfunction, no marked GI/hepatic dysfunction
Atrial fibrillation of other aetiology — the AF is a consequence of thyrotoxicosis rather than a primary diagnosis
Phaeochromocytoma — considered for adrenergic symptoms but no paroxysmal hypertension/headache/sweating crises
Anxiety/panic disorder — does not explain biochemical thyrotoxicosis, goitre or weight loss
finalDiagnosis: Uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis (biochemically confirmed hyperthyroidism, most consistent with amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis) presenting with new atrial fibrillation in an elderly peri-operative patient — not thyroid storm.
citations: American Thyroid Association (ATA) — Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis, 2016
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Hyperthyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis
stewardship: Not applicable — this is a non-infective endocrine presentation. No antimicrobial therapy is indicated; antibiotics would represent inappropriate use. Focus is on rate control, beta-blockade, antithyroid therapy and safe peri-operative optimisation.
contraindications: Avoid non-cardioselective high-dose beta-blockade if occult heart failure; assess volume status first
Radioiodine uptake diagnostics and radioactive iodine therapy are unreliable/contraindicated for months after amiodarone iodine load
Elective surgery should be deferred until the patient is rendered euthyroid to avoid precipitating thyroid storm perioperatively
Review/withhold amiodarone in discussion with cardiology given its role as the likely precipitant
edgeCases: Apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly may present mainly with AF and weight loss rather than classic hyperadrenergic features
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 1 vs type 2 distinction changes therapy (antithyroid drug vs corticosteroid)
New AF on background anticoagulation — confirm apixaban dosing appropriate for age/renal function
Distinguish uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis from thyroid storm using Burch-Wartofsky criteria before escalating care
expectedMaiK: Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 and free T3 in an elderly amiodarone-treated patient with new AF and weight loss = uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis; render euthyroid before elective surgery, not a septic or storm pathway.
expectedNextQuestions: Duration and dose of amiodarone, and any prior thyroid function tests?
Any eye symptoms, neck pain, or preceding viral illness to distinguish Graves vs thyroiditis vs amiodarone effect?
Symptoms of thyroid storm — fever, confusion, vomiting, diarrhoea severity, heart failure?
Family history of thyroid disease and current full medication list for interactions?
expectedInvestigations: TSH, free T4 and free T3
Interleukin-6 / distinguishing AIT type 1 vs type 2 work-up; baseline LFTs and FBC before antithyroid drugs
regressionAssertions: Engine must return hyperthyroidism as the top diagnosis
Must NOT trigger thyroid_storm (patient afebrile, GCS 15, low Burch-Wartofsky)
Must NOT recommend any antibiotic or sepsis pathway
Must flag suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3 as diagnostic
